summary: Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday evening—exceeding its previously marketed $70 to $78 range—as its shares prepare to begin trading today on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT".

By selling 980 million shares at $83 apiece, the offering raises approximately $81.34 billion, officially surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion initial debut from June to become the largest initial public offering on record.
The final pricing gives the Claude maker a fully diluted market valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion, positioning it among the world's most valuable public companies ahead of its opening bell.

Combined with a separate $26 billion private placement from major technology backers—including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, and AMD—Anthropic's total capitalization around the listing exceeds $105 billion before fees.

The record-breaking debut lands during a volatile stretch for technology equities, serving as a critical test of institutional appetite for pure-play artificial intelligence stocks amid heightened scrutiny over massive data center capital expenditures.
title: Source Icon

summary: On Thursday, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping , and Vladimir Putin concluded a 90-minute trilateral summit in Shenzhen, releasing a joint four-point statement on United Nations reform, refined petroleum supplies, state-official immunity, and nuclear dialogue.

Comparisons to the 1945 Yalta Conference surfaced, where Allied leaders reshaped the post-Second World War order; ahead of the talks, an official warned against a "redistribution of influence" among the three powers.

Leaders committed to United Nations reform and pledged to increase refined petroleum production while "engaging in dialogue" on nuclear risks; they also affirmed "respect for the immunity of state officials" against International Criminal Court overreach.

Chinese officials blocked a reporter from the trilateral opening after a question about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang; footage captured Putin telling Xi that "I don't think anyone even expected things to go so well."

Asia correspondent Helen-Ann Smith notes the talks are "unlikely" to have secured major breakthroughs, despite "historic significance" emphasized by leaders; the meeting raised concerns for Kyiv and Taipei over the shifting geopolitical landscape.
title: Trump, Xi and Putin Pledge UN Reforms, Increased Fuel Supplies and Nuclear Dialogue at Historic Meeting

summary: On Wednesday, November 18, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries secured the Democratic nomination for speaker in a 251-11 closed-door vote, positioning him to become the first Black speaker of the House.

The nomination solidifies a new leadership team in the post-Pelosi era, with Majority Leader-designate Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Majority Whip-designate Pete Aguilar of California poised to hold historic firsts.

Despite the decisive tally, seven incoming progressive lawmakers issued a statement opposing Jeffries' nomination, citing unaddressed demands regarding Medicare for All, immigration enforcement, and the conflict in Gaza.
Jeffries must still secure 218 votes on the House floor when the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, though his comfortable caucus margin suggests he is well-positioned to claim the gavel.

With Democrats poised to hold one of the largest majorities in decades, the party plans to prioritize an affordable America agenda while preparing to investigate the administration of President Donald Trump.
title: Democrats formally nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, paving way for him to be the first Black speaker

summary: On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin convened in Shenzhen for their first-ever trilateral summit, addressing nuclear arms, trade, and regional conflicts.

Xi greeted Trump at the airport with a hug, breaking diplomatic protocol, while Putin arrived separately; analysts characterize the summit as primarily symbolic with low expectations for substantive breakthroughs.

Discussions addressed nuclear security, Ukraine's war, and Iran, with Beijing maintaining that Washington and Moscow must reduce their arsenals before it agrees to cap its smaller stockpile of around 600 warheads.

European officials expressed alarm that regional security could be negotiated without their input, while technical outages at Microsoft and the Federal Aviation Administration undermined the administration's ability to project strength.

Trump and Xi plan to meet in December at the G20 Leaders' Summit in Miami, with analysts expecting Washington and Beijing to maintain relatively stable ties despite ongoing trade and technology tensions.
title: Trump lands in China for historic meeting with Xi, Putin

summary: On Tuesday, Nov. 17, Democrat Mary Peltola unseated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, flipping Alaska's Senate seat to Democratic control for the first time in 18 years and marking the ninth seat Democrats flipped this midterm.

Allegations that Peltola's campaign recruited retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan as a spoiler candidate roiled the race, prompting Trump to order the Justice Department to sue to block certification if the incumbent lost.

Peltola secured 50% of first-choice votes, rendering ranked-choice tabulation unnecessary; a federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit on Nov. 1, ruling such action would "clearly violate" voters' ballot secrecy rights.

With 56 seats, Democrats hold their largest Senate majority in 16 years when the new Congress convenes, surpassing the 53-47 margin Republicans held before the midterms and completing a nine-seat wave.

Peltola will become the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. Senate , sharing this historic milestone with Minnesota Democratic Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, marking a breakthrough for Indigenous representation in Congress.
title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins US Senate race in Alaska, beating incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan

summary: On Tuesday, The White House withdrew Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration after determining she lacked sufficient Senate support.
Her nomination faced bipartisan resistance in Congress, alongside criticism from Antiabortion forces and supporters of Health Secretary Robert Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again movement.
Previously expressing "strong concerns," Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, chairman of the Senate Health and Pensions Committee, called Overton's role "almost disqualifying."
Officials stated the White House intends to "go in a new direction at FDA " while continuing to support Kennedy's health agenda, necessitating a new candidate search.
Since Marty Makary's resignation in May, the agency has operated under acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, leaving the administration to identify a replacement to lead the FDA.
title: Trump’s pick Heidi Overton dropped as nominee for FDA commissioner

summary: On Wednesday, Skydance announced it will combine Warner Bros . Television Group and Paramount Television Studios into a single entity called Warner Bros. Television Studios, effective in early 2027.

Warner Bros. Television Group chief Channing Dungey and Paramount Television Studios head Matt Thunell will serve as co-presidents, reporting to Skydance Television Chief George Cheeks and overseeing scripted, unscripted, and BET Studios programming.

Skydance aims to achieve at least $6 billion in merger-related cost savings while servicing nearly $80 billion in net debt; consolidation is expected to lead to layoffs as duplicating jobs are eliminated.
Separately, President David Stapf will continue leading CBS Studios as a standalone entity under Cheeks, producing broadcast hits including 'NCIS' and 'FBI'.
The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will house more than 120 active series and major franchises including 'Ted Lasso,' 'The Pitt,' and the upcoming series 'Neuromancer'.
title: Skydance to combine Warner Bros. TV Group and Paramount Television Studios

title: Israel says it concludes Gaza tank raid

summary: A simulated emergency alert from FEMA on Tuesday triggered false narratives about worldwide blackouts that circulated rapidly across Spanish-language platforms within global Latino communities.
Service outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and the National Security Agency preceded the test; online actors distorted these real events as alleged evidence of an impending catastrophe.

The DDIA analyzed over 2,200 Spanish-language posts between Nov 11 and Nov 17, finding that content with 'alarmist headlines' amassed over 95 million views across mainstream and clickbait-style outlets.
Misinformation campaigns targeting Latinos exploited cultural sentiments, referencing Bad Bunny's track 'El Apagón' to frame power outages as ubiquitous hardships rather than just viral threats.

Experts Rafael Olavarría and Arthur Soto-Vásquez note this vulnerability stems from historical distrust of authority, suggesting the incident offers audiences an opportunity to examine their online information sources.
title: Misinformation about a FEMA test leveraged distrust in Spanish-speaking communities

summary: On Wednesday, former Cleveland Browns quarterback Bernie Kosar marked one year since his life-saving liver transplant, appearing at University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center with his granddaughter, Alia Rose Kosar-Beck.

Kosar received the organ from 21-year-old Bryce Dunlap of North Olmsted on November 17, 2025, after battling liver failure and Parkinson's disease diagnosed in 2024; the Dunlap family requested a directed donation.

Dr. Zoe Stewart Lewis, chief of transplant surgery, called Kosar 'the model patient' whose mental clarity improved significantly; he reduced daily medication from 50 pills and maintains blood tests every six weeks.
"What a difference a year makes," Kosar said, reflecting on his improved quality of life; he committed to advocating for organ donation and helping former athletes affected by cognitive issues.
As Kosar approaches his 63rd birthday next Wednesday, he remains dedicated to honoring Dunlap's memory and inspiring others through his recovery journey and second chance at life.
title: Bernie Kosar marks 1 year since liver transplant, says he feels ‘happily surprised’

summary: On Monday, Vice President JD Vance expressed willingness to work with Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, softening his tone after a contentious election season. The two are scheduled to meet at the U.S. Capitol on January 3, 2027, for the swearing-in ceremony.

Vance told Fox News that if El-Sayed wants to work to make lives better, he will "find us a very willing partner." El-Sayed responded, "For me, it will always be about serving working people."
Addressing Vance as "Habibi," an Arabic term meaning "my beloved," El-Sayed noted the irony that Vance is constitutionally obligated to swear him in. His victory speech drew laughter from supporters.

El-Sayed emphasized policy priorities including "Medicare for all" and getting "money out of politics" during his campaign. He also extended an invitation to Trump on NPR's Newsmakers, saying there is "a lot we could work on.
title: Vance and El-Sayed Are Looking to Meet After a Bitter, Personal Campaign Season

summary: Idaho Fish and Game Commissioner Brody Harshbarger agreed to plead guilty to two misdemeanor hunting charges—hunting without a valid tag and shooting across a road—in exchange for prosecutors dropping poaching and trespassing counts.

The charges stemmed from a December 20, 2025, incident in Fremont County, where Harshbarger and Eric Murphy allegedly killed two bull elk unlawfully near Spring Hollow boat ramp without permission to shoot on the property.

Under the plea agreement, Harshbarger faces a $500 fine for each of the two charges and a one-year revocation of hunting privileges, with sentencing scheduled for December 9, 2026, according to court records.

Although Harshbarger remains an Idaho Fish and Game commissioner, his profile was removed from the agency's website on Monday, and Governor Brad Little is working to ensure the position's responsibilities are fulfilled.

Calling it an 'extremely important matter,' Sheryl Hill of Ashton said hunters have remained unrepresented on the commission since charges were filed, prompting public calls for answers regarding representation.
title: Idaho Fish and Game Commissioner to Plead Guilty on Hunting Charges, Prompting Calls for Accountability

summary: On Thursday, November 19, 2026, convicted killer Susan Smith will appear before the South Carolina Board of Paroles and Pardons seeking release for her 1995 life sentence for drowning her two sons in 1994.
Smith initially claimed a man carjacked her vehicle, sparking a nationwide search before she confessed nine days later to letting her car roll into John D. Long Lake with her boys trapped inside.

Urging the board to deny her release, ex-husband David Smith plans to attend the hearing and vowed to keep her behind bars for life. "I will be here every two years going forward," David told the board.

The South Carolina Board of Paroles and Pardons unanimously rejected Smith's first request in 2024, and members are expected to consider the crime 's severity and her prison conduct, including disciplinary violations.

Currently working as a wardkeeper at Leath Correctional Institution, Smith remains eligible for parole every two years until released or deceased, even as prosecutors and family members continue to oppose her freedom.
title: Susan Smith to ask for parole again 32 years after drowning her sons in a South Carolina lake

summary: On Friday, Nov. 20, the U.S. Army will conduct two controlled detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown at approximately noon to destroy degraded lead azide explosives.
Army spokesperson Justine Barati noted the operation targets 68 barrels of lead azide stored for nearly 20 years, which crystallized and became too unstable to move safely.
Residents in Middletown City Park must vacate from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday as a precaution due to potential localized window damage from the consecutive, rapid detonations.
Families and pets can find shelter at the Armed Forces Reserve Center at 16815 U.S. 34 in Middletown, which offers refreshments and gym facilities during the operation.
Modeling predicts an airborne plume up to 20 miles wide, and the Environmental Protection Agency permitted the operation under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act with hourly map updates.
title: Lead From Army Detonation in Iowa Town Could Pose Health Risks

summary: On Wednesday, the GEO Group sold the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma , Washington, to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for $453 million, shifting ownership from private operator to federal government.
Despite federal ownership, GEO will continue operating the facility under a new 10-year, $1.5 billion contract running through Oct. 27, 2036, maintaining day-to-day management and staffing services.
The 1,635-bed facility's sale yields approximately $340 million in net proceeds after taxes and fees, which GEO plans to deploy toward a $500 million accelerated share repurchase program.

U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal, Ranking Member of the House Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, fears the government overpaid, citing Tacoma's $72.6 million property assessment and warning federal ownership could bypass state oversight.

La Resistencia, an immigrant rights organization, vows to continue fighting for permanent facility closure, while GEO remains in "active negotiation" to sell three additional company-owned facilities to DHS before year-end.
title: ICE Buys Washington Immigrant Detention Center From GEO Group for $453 Million

summary: The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus scheduled a news conference for Thursday to demand a legislative inquiry into over 230,000 voters marked inactive ahead of the November midterm elections, an increase of nearly 60,000 since the presidential election two years ago.

Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson announced a partnership with Experian in 2025 intended to strengthen election integrity by using credit and Social Security data alongside Postal Service records to verify voter addresses.

Voters marked inactive had to cast provisional ballots; statewide approval reached 75%, but Associated Press data shows the rate dropped to 34% in Hinds County, home to Jackson, compared with 60% there in 2024.

State Rep. Cheikh Taylor, chair of the Mississippi Democratic Party , plans to introduce legislation increasing transparency in credit-data use and allowing voters to confirm identities before deactivation. Republican state senator Jeremy England suggested the proposal could draw bipartisan support.

Democrats seek to prevent what they termed "disenfranchisement" by ensuring eligible voters are not mistakenly deactivated as they build momentum ahead of next year's race for governor, where multiple statewide offices will be contested.
title: Mississippi Democrats Seek Inquiry Into Surge in Inactive Voters

Despite public concern over technology outages, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Clayton confirmed there is no evidence linking recent disruptions at the Federal Aviation Administration and Microsoft to Iranian cyberattacks.
U.S. forces struck an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile site on Qeshm Island last Tuesday, following multiple Iranian attacks on radar facilities in Bahrain that caused little damage.
Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio stated Wednesday there was "no credible threat" to Washington, while the White House reinforced that assessment in a separate statement.

Intelligence reports suggesting Iran discussed a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington fueled public anxiety despite Tehran's denials, though FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia labeled such reporting "aspirational" while monitoring advanced-stage plotting.
title: Threats from Iran have increased substantially, US intelligence director says

summary: Denmark’s parliament unanimously ratified a trilateral defense agreement with the United States and Greenland on Thursday—passing by a 109–0 vote in the Folketing—to expand the American military footprint across the strategic Arctic island.

Signed in September to amend and supplement the foundational 1951 defense pact, the executive agreement permits Washington to modernize Pituffik Space Base, establish additional defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, and deploy elements of its "Golden Dome" missile defense system.

The pact resolves months of intense transatlantic friction sparked earlier this year when U.S. President Donald Trump refused to rule out military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous territory on national security grounds.

While formally preserving Danish sovereignty and recognizing Greenlanders’ right to self-determination, the treaty remains permanently binding even if Greenland later chooses independence, requires local procurement for base construction where possible, and bars non-NATO powers from establishing installations on the island.

Following approval by Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, earlier this month in a 16–0 vote with seven abstentions, the agreement will formally enter into force once Copenhagen delivers diplomatic notification to Washington.
title: Danish Parliament Approves Defense Deal Expanding U.S. Military Presence in Greenland

summary: Sixteen Ecuadorian fishers are suing the American government in District Court on Monday, alleging forces abducted and tortured them after a March 17 drone strike sank their boat, the Negra Francisca Duarte.

The lawsuit targets Operation Southern Spear, an administration boat-strike campaign launched in late 2025, which the Washington Office estimates has killed at least 238 people while officials provide scant evidence of narcotics trafficking.

Two armed drones destroyed the vessel 385 nautical miles from Manta, Ecuador , on March 17, severely burning two crew members, despite prior Ecuadorian authorities' inspections confirming the boat carried no drugs.

Survivors claim uniformed personnel hooded and jailed them for weeks in El Salvador; Dan Kovalik, the attorney representing the fishermen, says the men seek accountability from the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress for the "manifestly unlawful" attacks.

This filing joins mounting legal challenges, including a wrongful death lawsuit from Trinidadian fishers and an ACLU Freedom of Information Act suit demanding release of secret Justice Department legal opinions justifying the strikes.
title: 16 Ecuadorian Fishermen File Lawsuit Against Trump Administration Over U.S. Military Strike and Detention

summary: The Federal Communications Commission will vote Thursday on a regulation change allowing state and local prisons to use jamming technology against contraband cellphones, according to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

Inmates have used smuggled devices to order violence, drug operations, and kidnappings, prompting South Carolina leaders and federal officials to push for years to change the law allowing jamming in state prisons.

Captain Robert Johnson, a corrections officer shot six times in a 2010 hit ordered by an inmate, called the phones "weapons of mass destruction" at Wednesday's press conference after undergoing 38 surgeries.

South Carolina Department of Corrections Director Joel Anderson said the state will immediately submit an application to implement jamming at Broad River Correctional Facility in Columbia once the FCC approves the change.

While telecommunications groups and inmate advocates have opposed jamming over interference concerns, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said opposition has waned as technology improved, allowing precise signal blocking confined to prison grounds.
title: FCC Expected to Allow State Prisons to Jam Contraband Cellphone Signals with Thursday Vote – WTOP News

summary: On Thursday, November 19, 2026, Florida is scheduled to execute Thomas Overton at Florida State Prison, marking the state's 20th execution this year and setting a new annual record.

Overton, an Army veteran and survivor of the abusive Dozier School, was sentenced for the 1991 murders of Michael and Susan MacIvor; attorneys allege the investigation involved "extraordinary failures" including mishandled DNA evidence and psychic contamination.

His legal team filed a Supreme Court petition challenging Florida's clemency system, arguing the "clemency process as it was originally intended no longer exists." The jury recommended death sentences by non-unanimous votes of 9-3 and 8-4.

Governor Ron DeSantis has overseen record executions; Overton will be the 15th military veteran put to death under his administration. Advocates recently urged Governor-elect Byron Donalds to halt future proceedings after taking office in January.

A recent Gallup poll found national support for capital punishment has dipped below 50 percent for the first time since 1971. Other states like Ohio and Pennsylvania have recently moved to review or commute death sentences amid the national shift.
title: Florida set to carry out its record-breaking 20th execution same day as a Texas lethal injection

summary: On March 9, Hachette Book Group imprint Center Street will publish "Redeem the Time: The Strange Gift of Dying and the Lost Art of Living," co-authored by former Senator Ben Sasse and his daughter, Alex Sasse.
Sasse, 54, announced in December 2025 that he was diagnosed with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer; after doctors gave him four months to live, he completed the memoir in hospital hallways.
The memoir reflects on time, workaholism, and family rather than being a standard cancer narrative, as Sasse notes the "gift of dying" shatters the "insane delusions of self-control."
Center Street describes the work as a "poignant book that reflects on many of these themes," including the need for family and embodied communities in an era of digital rootlessness.
Sasse previously served as president of the University of Florida and authored "Them: Why We Hate Each Other and How to Heal" and "The Vanishing American Adult.
title: Former Sen. Ben Sasse’s memoir on surviving cancer, co-written with his daughter, is set for March 9

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Paxton’s action chiefly as “abandoning” an effort to “ban” CAIR, linking it to a Democratic “sweep” and emphasizing civil-liberties concerns; center coverage adds CAIR’s identity as a Muslim civil-rights group, the proposed “terrorist organization” designation, the lack of a judicial ruling, and Abbott’s separate designation.

Right-Leaning accounts portray a major attempt to “shut down” CAIR and the “Muslim Brotherhood,” stress the procedural “without prejudice” filing, and use emphatic “DROPS” while attributing the retreat to Democratic victories.
All agree the lawsuit ended, but their dividing line is whether that outcome signals political retreat, civil-rights protection, or unresolved security claims amid broader partisan conflict.
summary: On Monday, outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a notice of nonsuit, ending his Collin County lawsuit against the Council on American-Islamic Relations. The move follows Paxton's loss in his U.S. Senate race.

Allegations in the February filing claimed the Council functioned as a 'front group' for Hamas and sought to advance Sharia law. Gov. Greg Abbott had previously issued a state proclamation labeling the group a terrorist organization.

Paxton's office has recently abandoned lawsuits targeting the NCAA over transgender athletes, marking a broader retreat from politically charged cases. CAIR previously rejected the state's accusations as retaliation for its political advocacy.
Although the lawsuit is dismissed, Abbott's designation remains in effect as a separate issue. Incoming Gov. Gina Hinojosa has pledged to remove the label when she assumes office.

Hinojosa told the Washington Post, 'We have to use public safety measures for public safety,' dismissing what she called political misuse of power. Mustafaa Carroll, CAIR-Dallas executive director, expressed hope for unity under the incoming administration.
title: Ken Paxton’s Office Drops Lawsuit Seeking to Ban Muslim Civil Rights Group in Texas

bias: Coverage is broadly positive but diverges in emphasis: left-leaning accounts portray Walmart ’s growth as broad-based, driven by inflation-weary shoppers seeking cheaper groceries and gas, with upbeat language such as “solid,” “growing number,” and a “flywheel” gathering momentum; right-leaning coverage frames upper-income households as the force that “fuel” sales and “led” market-share gains, adding scale through $188.8 billion in global revenue and 5.2% growth.

Center coverage bridges the narratives, highlighting the third outlook increase while stressing a “cautious outlook.” The dividing line is whether Walmart’s success reflects broad consumer cost pressure or affluent-market strength; all agree sales rose and guidance improved, reflecting wider debates over inflation, class, and economic resilience.
summary: On Thursday, Walmart reported $188.8 billion in revenue, a 5.2% increase, and raised its full-year guidance for the third time this year.
Upper-Income households drove the performance, while the retailer launched a $120 membership bundle combining Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus ahead of the holidays.
Global e-commerce sales rose 17% and U.S. online sales jumped 23%, though federal legislation requiring capped prices on high-cost Medicare drugs weighed on comparable sales.
Walmart CEO John Furner stated the company is "growing our core business and gaining market share," though the raised outlook was more conservative than some analysts expected.
Analysts look to the retailer as a barometer for the broader economy, tracking how resilient households prioritize value as shoppers become more selective with holiday spending.
title: Walmart raises sales and earnings outlook as e-commerce sales jump again

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the breach as an urgent privacy and security threat, using phrases like “quietly slipped into,” “hackers,” and “sensitive” data while suggesting attackers sought settlement funds and invoking broader cyberattack concerns.
Right-Leaning coverage narrows the issue to unauthorized access, stressing that no evidence shows retirees’ money was “stolen,” thereby separating exposure from confirmed financial loss.

Center coverage emphasizes operational context—Atticus Administration, settlement payments, and the approximately $53 million settlement—while using restrained terms such as “accessed” and “compromised.” All perspectives highlight financial and medical information affecting up to 4,000 retirees, but their divide reflects competing concerns over privacy risk, institutional vulnerability, and evidentiary caution.
summary: On Thursday, Politico reported that hackers accessed financial and health data of 4,000 retired New York City government workers through Atticus Administration, which manages a $53 million settlement with EmblemHealth.
Retirees submitted claims for co-pay reimbursements under the GHI Senior Care plan for 2022 and 2023, creating the database that hackers infiltrated this fall.
After Atticus flagged submissions as "invalid" on October 12, 2026, the company confirmed with disbursement partners that "no claimant payout was created, changed or redirected" during the breach.
Spokesperson Alex Gomez confirmed Wednesday that Emblem's investigation is ongoing, and officials stated that claims processing and distribution will continue despite the breach.
The identity of the hackers and their motive remain publicly unknown, highlighting broader cybersecurity risks when governments rely on third-party contractors to handle sensitive information.
title: Hackers access financial data of retired NYC government workers, Politico reports
topic_full: New York State Politics · New York

summary: Campbell County denied on Monday that jail staff caused Kenneth Durrah's death, arguing in court filings that his 2022 passing resulted from his own concealed drug ingestion rather than deputies' use of force or inadequate medical care.

The civil rights lawsuit alleges law enforcement used excessive force and showed deliberate indifference to Durrah's medical needs before he died at the Campbell County Detention Center on Dec. 1, 2022, while strapped to a restraint chair.

Video footage shows Durrah telling Detention Officer Samuel Boyles, "It's too tight, please," while restrained. Deputies left him in the chair for half an hour without summoning medical aid after witnessing him ingest suspected methamphetamine, the complaint states.

Defending their actions, the county argues the strip search and restraint chair were justified by Durrah's resistance and suspected contraband. Defense disputes deliberate indifference claims, asserting staff began CPR and applied an AED when they found him unresponsive.

An autopsy described the cause of death as "sudden cardiac death, consistent with" excited delirium due to methamphetamine, but the lawsuit argues prone restraint produced a fatal chemical imbalance that deputies failed to mitigate.
title: Campbell County blames meth, denies excessive force in fatal jail restraint lawsuit

bias: Left-Leaning coverage dramatizes the incident through phrases like “dark web hackers” and “richest clients,” foregrounding the alleged leak of roughly 16,000 customers’ data and its populist implications.
Center coverage moderates that alarm by distinguishing vendor-held marketing data from JPMorgan’s core systems and specifying possible names, emails, phone numbers, and account IDs.
Right-Leaning coverage de-emphasizes the leak, repeating that third-party vendors were “targeted” and framing the episode as limited in scope.

The pivotal divide is whether this is a consequential privacy breach or a vendor-level attack; all perspectives agree that third-party providers were attacked, reflecting broader differences over institutional risk and accountability.
summary: On Thursday, JPMorgan Chase announced that third-party vendors providing services to the firm were targeted by a cyberattack, though the bank confirmed there is no disruption to its own services.
Investigation findings suggest attackers accessed 'certain marketing data' held by the vendors, which may include customer names and email addresses.
A spokesperson told Reuters there is 'no connection to the service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week' when technical issues affected multiple banks.
JPMorgan will contact impacted customers directly to offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring, as it addresses the security incident.

These incidents follow several recent technical problems, including a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop last week, Microsoft's global email outage, and a massive hack at Binance last month.
title: JPMorganChase reports cyberattack on third-party service providers

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Nazi persecution, possible dispossession, and a “dark cloud” over the sale, portraying the £145 million result as ethically troubling.

Right-Leaning framing stresses Sotheby’s claim that no evidence established duress, uses phrases like “shaky ground,” “risk-taking,” and “eye-watering” to cast the heirs’ challenge as legally uncertain yet commercially dramatic.
Center coverage treats the provenance dispute as a “complex past,” emphasizing the last-minute agreement and market implications.
The pivotal divide is whether settlement resolves injustice or merely permits trading amid unresolved history.
All emphasize the $190.4 million record, reflecting tensions between restitution, property rights, and commerce.
summary: On Wednesday night, Vincent van Gogh 's painting of blossoming chestnut trees sold for $190.4 million at Sotheby's in Manhattan, ending an eleventh-hour dispute after the Blaquier-Arrieta family and heirs of Samuel Fischer reached a Monday settlement.

Heirs of Samuel Fischer staked a claim last week, alleging the painting was sold in 1936 under duress of Nazi persecution; lawyer Gunnar Schnabel represented their interests in negotiations that preceded the auction.

All 12 works from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection sold for $412 million, falling short of Sotheby's $450 million estimate, with other notable sales including a Paul Cézanne painting for $111 million and a Camille Pissaro cityscape for $24.2 million.

Art adviser Ralph DeLuca noted the auction room felt "tepid," with "no mood, no Champagne atmosphere," yet the final results offer evidence of the high-end art market's cautious recovery from a yearslong recession.

The 1890 canvas set an auction record for Van Gogh and became the sixth most expensive painting ever sold at auction when adjusted for inflation, surpassing the previous record of $117.2 million set in 2022 for a landscape from Paul Allen's collection.
title: Van Gogh Painting Sells for Record $190.4m After Dispute

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the bishops’ AI task force around “ regulation ,” “guardrails,” and “worker protections,” presenting oversight as necessary to “protect humanity” and addressing employment risks.

Right-Leaning coverage shifts from labor policy to moral authority: “must” and “control” emphasize human command, while “the clock is ticking” adds urgency and “human dignity” and “the common good” invoke tradition.
Center coverage links the initiative to Pope Leo’s warning that AI is the “biggest challenge today” and calls for “robust” regulation.
Despite these divides, all portray the task force, safeguards, and human welfare as essential amid broader technological and cultural anxieties.
summary: On Wednesday, November 18, Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, California, urged the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops in Baltimore to ensure humans maintain control over artificial intelligence to safeguard human dignity and the common good.

Bishop Cantú leads the newly formed USCCB task force, which seeks to implement Pope Leo's vision from the encyclical 'Magnifica Humanitas' to keep technology rooted in human dignity and Catholic social teaching.

The task force will provide webinars and become a clearinghouse for best practices while advocating for 'clear guardrails on the development and use of AI,' including transparency, accountability, and human oversight.

With technology expected to reach full speed within six months to a year, the Church is engaging major technology companies, which have expressed 'genuine openness to dialogue' regarding moral and ethical questions at stake.

The Church aims to become a 'school of discernment in the digital age' to protect vulnerable persons, while insisting that 'moral responsibility in conflict cannot be delegated to an algorithm,' Cantú said.
title: US Catholic bishops’ new AI task force urges regulation and worker protections

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the mosque fire as “settler terror,” “organized Zionist terrorism,” and part of a wider pattern of occupation, anti-Arab violence, and displacement, foregrounding alleged masked attackers, a Molotov cocktail, Shin Bet involvement, and “far-right incitement.” Right-leaning coverage narrows the event to a “suspected hate crime ,” retaining uncertainty while emphasizing law-and-order concerns and accusations of “incitement” tied to Netanyahu’s camp.
Center coverage similarly stresses a police probe and religious desecration without assigning definitive blame.

The pivotal divide is whether the fire represents systemic settler violence or an isolated suspected crime; all perspectives acknowledge the fire, nationalist graffiti, investigation, and communal danger.
summary: On Thursday morning, a fire broke out at a mosque near Afula, prompting the Shin Bet and Israel Police to launch an investigation into a suspected hate crime . Firefighters from Israel Fire and the Rescue Authority extinguished the blaze.

Nationalist and anti-Islamic graffiti slogans, including the word 'revenge' in Hebrew, were found sprayed on the mosque walls. The incident follows a suspected nationalist car-ramming attack in Kafr Kassem on Wednesday evening that wounded at least three people.

The mosque's imam told Walla that three attackers arrived carrying a Molotov cocktail and gasoline, spray-painted 'revenge,' then set the building on fire. Fortunately, the blaze was not intense, and the imam and others extinguished it upon arrival for prayers.

"I am not concerned that this incident will lead to unrest," the imam stated, adding that the community has spoken with the Israel Police, who have collected evidence and are working to apprehend the attackers.

Investigators are examining how the suspects reached the village near Afula, with one possibility being they arrived on foot through forests adjacent to the site. The Rescue Services are also analyzing the circumstances of the fire.
title: Israel Police probe suspected arson attack on mosque near Afula, nationalist graffiti found

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the event as intentional anti-Palestinian violence, stressing “settler,” “deliberate,” and “terrorist act,” while emphasizing Israeli identity and Palestinian victimization.

Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds the arrest, “ramming incident,” possible drug impairment, and procedural investigation, though its secondary use of “deliberate manslaughter” and “occupied Arab territories” introduces sharper political language.
The pivotal divide is whether the vehicle strikes constitute terrorism or loss of control—a question center coverage presents as unresolved through “hit-and-run” and competing explanations.

Across perspectives, reports emphasize at least eight injuries at multiple locations and an investigation, reflecting broader disputes over intent, accountability, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
summary: A driver struck eight Palestinians in Kafr Qassem on Wednesday, injuring victims who required immediate hospital transport for treatment.
Initial reports identify the driver as a Jewish Israeli settler, with the incident occurring in the Arab town of Kafr Qasim in central Israel.
Surveillance footage documents the vehicle striking two individuals, providing visual evidence of the hit-and-run incident as it unfolded across the town.
Several victims received hospital treatment for moderate injuries. An eyewitness described "hysteria" and people in panic after hearing screams near an event hall.
Israel Police are examining several lines of inquiry, including potential intoxication or a nationalistic motive, while keeping all possibilities open as investigation continues.
title: Jewish Israeli arrested after ramming at least eight in Kafr Kassem hit-and-run

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump’s refusal to promise pressure on China as inconsistency, calling his claim that America spies “better” a “boast” while stressing business ties and the stakes of a “key trip.” Right-leaning coverage instead amplifies confidence through “I KNOW EVERYTHING,” “spy better,” and a “positive development,” portraying reciprocal espionage as strategic strength and de-emphasizing the refusal itself.
Center coverage uses attribution—“claims” and “upper hand”—to temper the assertion without endorsing it.

The dividing line is whether espionage signals hypocrisy, cautious pragmatism, or national advantage; all perspectives nonetheless emphasize mutual spying, the Xi meeting, and rivalry shaped by competing economic and geopolitical priorities.
summary: On Wednesday, President Donald Trump , currently in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, said he would not press China to stop spying on the nation because both countries engage in mutual intelligence gathering.

Trump defended the intelligence rivalry, stating, "We spy on them...we spy on China, they spy on us." He claimed deep business ties with Beijing make the surveillance relationship a reality of international commerce.

These remarks followed reports involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a businesswoman Chinese intelligence suspects has ties to spying. The scandal reached the White House and threatened Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Trump dismissed the Nvidia scandal as a "tragedy," calling Jensen Huang a "brilliant man" despite intelligence concerns. Separately, he downplayed recent technology outages at Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and United Airlines as routine equipment installation issues.
High-Stakes meetings with Chinese President Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin remain on Trump's agenda in Shenzhen, where he intends to discuss ending the war in Iran and denuclearization.
title: Trump says US, China spy on each other, claims US does it better

bias: Coverage diverges mainly in emphasis: center-leaning accounts foreground Tesla ’s planned production increase and Musk’s warning about “geopolitical potholes” linked to Taiwan, while right-leaning coverage spotlights cordial China ties, his son’s visit, and phrases like “superfan,” “toy paradise,” and “cute moment.” The same Taiwan reference becomes a strategic risk in one framing but a veiled statement confronting China’s “red line” in the other.
Center coverage treats “pledges” and “boost” cautiously, whereas the right stresses personal enthusiasm and spectacle.

Both portray Musk’s China favorably and report continued Shanghai output, reflecting shared attention to manufacturing dependence and the wider tension between commercial engagement and geopolitical suspicion.
summary: Elon Musk said Tesla would continue increasing output at its Shanghai factory, according to Yuyuan Tantian, a social media account affiliated with China’s state broadcaster CCTV.
Yuyuan Tantian reported that Musk made the remarks during a meeting with Ren Hongbin, head of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.
Tesla delivered 810,889 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles from its Shanghai plant in the first 10 months of the year, up 21.4% from a year earlier.
The factory can produce more than 950,000 vehicles annually, sources 98% of its parts from China, and exports vehicles to Europe, South Korea, and Australia.
title: Musk pledges higher Tesla output at China plant, Chinese state media says
